comments.name: Harry Baumgarten
comments.body:
Federal Aviation Regulations extract:

§ 91.119 Minimum safe altitudes: General.

Except when necessary for takeoff or landing, no person may operate an aircraft below the following altitudes:

(a) Anywhere. An altitude allowing, if a power unit fails, an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface.

(b) Over congested areas. Over any congested area of a city, town, or settlement, or over any open air assembly of persons, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft.

(c) Over other than congested areas. An altitude of 500 feet above the surface, except over open water or sparsely populated areas. In those cases, the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure.

The Blue Angels operate under specific FAA exemptions and airshow waivers allowing aerobatics and low-altitude flights, but these do not permit flying directly over crowds.

In that way, any rigging could only be done by 50 separate groups each having to create a custom approach according to the 50 different election rules and practices.  Whereas, federal operation could be rigged by a single group with a single strategy.

This rule isn’t an isolated case. It fits a broader pattern: OMB has long had the authority to capture, redirect, and condition taxpayer‑funded programs across agencies. Russell Vought used that authority during his tenure — apportionments, regulatory holds, cross‑agency alignment — and this proposal extends that approach into scientific research. The claim of “democratic control” doesn’t match the structure: OMB is not elected, its director is not elected, and the Heritage Foundation is not elected.

This is not the only taxpayer‑money pool he has attempted to capture or redistribute toward aligned interests. That’s standard operating procedure for OMB, and the public can see the pattern: administrative power being used to insert political review into domains that require expertise, while calling it democracy.

comments.name: Tom Brown
comments.body: The problem with people like Mr. Vought is that they assume that ideas or research findings that do not support their ideology are themselves necessarily ideological. Thus studies about racial disparities in health outcomes in the United States or the reality of anthropogenic climate change, however well supported empirically, get derided as "woke" or biased. It is much easier to allege "bias" or elitism than to deal with the underlying evidence. Better yet to cut off at the source research that might lead somewhere they don't want.  They will not admit the fact that in our advanced, highly technological society, knowledge is often specialized and key decisions about research, to be made competently, have to be made by people with demonstrated expertise in the relevant fields. They also have a deadly aversion to pluralism, our nation's strength, evidently because they lack the courage of their own convictions. All grant decisions need to be democratically accountable and so there is a natural tension here. But that is what Congress is for, and for Vought et. al to bypass the Congress and claim to be representing the people makes no sense. We need to be clear. This administration, in rampaging against the so-called "administrative state" and in its attacks on science, universities, the arts and humanities and the non-profit sector, is not upholding American "greatness". comments.name: Jack Haffey

The Democrats' view and the Democratic Socialists' view are both understandable. This comment posits that the real culprit in the United States is the underliving of our economic lives by adhering to shareholder primacy as the core driver of behavior. Professor Friedman created it as an imperative, Jensen and Meckling put it on steroids. It is bad because it created the primary issue that divides the two groups this article addresses, for one thing. More importantly it does not follow the full guidance Adam Smith gave us 250 years ago!
He effectively taught us that self-interest value maximization over the long run is a function of optimizing the value the firm provides to its primary stakeholder groups - the ones it affects in a significant and treasured way over time. They are customers, employees, suppliers, financial investors, communities where the firm has a presence and the general public interest. So, six (6) groups should be the primary focus of the firm.  If this imperative change is made to our capitalist economy's definition and behavior, the differences between the two groups discussed in this article would be narrowed, even eliminated. And the firms would do better over the long run as well. More to explain, but this conceptual, philosophical and actionable change to our economic system is the correction needed for far more than 50 years, and our Democratic Republic would itself be the other ultimate beneficiary!

Every day he awaits a breaking report that ICE agents have been killed making a pointless traffic stop only to find they picked armed individuals ready to resist, or a vehicle with passengers prepared to defend a cargo of drugs. His point is that we are one or two incidents away from  a shift toward bloody mayhem in the streets provoked by aggressive ICE behavior and thoughtless assumptions about the victims.

His worry underscores a more basic problem. All of the institutional constraints on proper procedure, warrants, due process, and what is often rebuked for  "choking the system" serves to reduce the threat of lethal violence affecting law enforcement, the justice system, and ordinary citizens. If I can count on institutions to function correctly, to protect my interests, then I can decide whether to trust them to assure I am treated fairly. If institutions are overwhelmed, broken, or subverted then I am at greater risk, whether from a mugger or an ICE agent. At some point, in the heat of a confrontation, it matters little whether  I am threatened by a common-variety thug or some version of a warrior cop. Unfortunately ICE personnel appeared encouraged to act as the first, which is why my son fears an inevitable hostile reaction.

It is perfectly reasonable to ask ICE to function as a law enforcement agency in accordance with professional standards.  Otherwise ICE threatens all of us by undermining justice institutions and promoting injustice.

Smoke inhalation is dangerous to adults, but especially dangerous to children with smaller airways that can more easily get narrowed substantially by swollen inner lining cells (the respiratory endothelium).
The nature of damage in children can be quite severe with special risks for infants who had respiratory complications in the nursery from Hyaline Membrane Disease (lung immaturity) or meconium aspiration (the inhaled amniotic fluid of a post-dates infant.

Asthmatic children, those with Bronchiectasis or with Cystic Fibrosis are especially at risk!

No extrapulmonary problems in children are known to my best understanding, but adults can be prone to problems of both heart and kidney problems as well.

https://www.columbiadoctors.org/news/wildfire-smoke-sending-more-people-hospital

If the level of particulate materials is very high, evidence exists from Nemmar and associates that the smoke particles can and do enter the bloodstream and are potentially capable of damaging organs from alteration of the vascular lining, the vascular endothelium.
https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/hc0402.104118

Wear the best quality mask you have access to for outdoor activities so long as the wildfire smoke is about.  N95 Masks can give substantial protection for the potential of dangers experienced, but spend as little time as possible out of doors in the areas at risk.

"...this discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves. articles.title: The Inside Story of IBM’s Shocking Profit Warning
articles.byline: Emily Glazer, Anissa Gardizy and Lauren Thomas
articles.summary: Big Blue bet on transparency and paid a steep price. Can its CEO win back investors?

comments.name: Patricia Miller
comments.body: So many investors (both large and small) are so often attracted to the moving light and frankly that's what I believe is happening with AI related companies at this moment.  No one really knows how this industry will eventually settle, and I don't mean turn staid - I do mean have a game plan that is understandable and achievable; one that can be projected into some reasonable "future".  Instead what we really have been seeing is the investing world (both big and small) appears to be looking for Hal to provide the guiding light insofar as AI is concerned.  IBM has configured itself and reconfigured itself successfully over many years and there is no reason to believe that they will fail to do so now.  But, since we live in the land of "what have you done for me lately" we will just have to ride out the current downside.

comments.name: David Walker
comments.body: The author presents this issue as a choice - it was not a choice. IBM became aware of material undisclosed information which was greatly at odds with guidance they had previously provided. Sitting on such information even a week or two after they knew it would be a huge mistake and surely they would have faced major lawsuits from shareholders.

comments.name: Edward D
comments.body:
IBM biggest Black Swan is Claude.AI 

If you look at the archaic, simple, workflow tools IBM license to corporations - Claude can easily reproduce those process and save corporations a lot of money supporting those processes in-house. 

IBM is toast - that's the real AI threat

comments.name: amish patel

comments.name: Thomas C
comments.body: Management's explanation for the quarter seems sound and hardly suggests their business is failing at the expense of AI.  No business lays on a straight line.  What is nuts is that the market took the stock from current levels in mid-May to a point where now we're having a spasm over it being down.  Why was it up?  Momentum and FOMO.

comments.name: David S

comments.name: Edward D

IBM is on the verge of cratering like Xerox except IBM totally hollowed itself out with outsourcing and the cheapest labor possible. 

The company failure began when they sold ThinkPad to Lenovo - the worst mistake in computing history.

comments.name: Nicolaus Henke
comments.body: IBM are on the wrong boat. They served menus at their company restaurants created by AI 15 years ago. They had Watson. They had Health. But they somehow missed to think about how AI can upgrade their legacy software and hardware business and most people wouldn’t know of relevant products IBM has created for this moment.

comments.name: Bob The Plumber
comments.body:
Just a few observations:
The article mentions the original building and the alterations would be designed to accommodate future live loads which were not yet present. I believe commercial office space assumes much higher loading than residential-so maybe the contractors thought they had a bit of a cushion. Also a frequent overloading situation occurs when drywall (Sheetrock) is loaded onto the floors.  
Another thing no one mentioned is that when the columns buckled the beam it was supporting may have “gone catenary”.  In other words the sagging beam could have acted like a suspension bridge. 
It’s often said that most improvements in construction technology occur after a major mishap. This may well lead to some improvements.

comments.name: Ed
comments.body:
It seems, if anything, that the developers, who are likely in a bit of trouble, were quite lucky.

It's one thing when the building partially collapses while under construction because its clearly not reinforced.  Imagine if the building had somehow managed to stay up until it was occupied by live people and their heavy things?  The thing could have been an absolute disaster.

comments.name: Neal Calvin
comments.body: I love how the design engineers are never actually there during construction. Some sort of legal expertise required to be a professional engineer now. Anyhow, it made me think of this Youtube animated video from The Efficient Engineer describing buckling! yay!

comments.name: A. Jones
comments.body: In reading this piece, I kept thinking about a contractor I have used for several remodeling projects and his attention to detail. He is upfront about cost---"this will cost some more, but you really should do it.." and thankfully, I do let him do it.

comments.name: Disillusioned1

comments.name: Galfrido

comments.name: Hafu

Somehow on a dead sprint (no walking!) he cushioned the long pass with his foot without changing the direction of the ball. Still sprinting ahead of the defender Messi allowed the ball to  bounce and then he flicked it up over the goaltender right in front of him so that the ball hit the underside of the top of the net. I've never seen anything like it. Poetry over physics. That's the only explanation.

The video of the museum from the air floored me- one picture’s worth 1000 words, right?  But those words got me to the video. The TR building is spectacular, but based on this article I don't see much reason to go inside. If the "papers" are all digitized only certain scholars would need to see the originals. comments.name: Bo Hodiak
comments.body: No doubt Sirski (my spelling) is uncomfortable with the high tech people, something he only partially understands. As one person wrote, World War I generals did not believe machine guns were lethal weapons. I'm sure money is part of the fight. Sirski has refused to allow funding for a number of Fedorov's projects. I hope Zelenski can get Fedorov back. Fedorov now is more important than Sirski.

comments.name: ed
comments.body: The people like Federov. This is important. Zelensky should really smooth things over publically and appoint him to a good position.

comments.name: JAB
comments.body:
A young technology-conversant minister vs an old-school brute-force general. Which is putting country over personal ambition and pride? We don’t know enough yet to answer the question. What we do know is based on what we observe.

The Russian-Ukraine War is asymmetrical. Russia has more weapons; more soldiers to expend. Because Trump attempted to tie Zelensky’s hands behind his back to favor Russia, Ukraine was forced to innovate.

Asymmetrical wars can be won by those smart enough to recognize when changes in strategy are needed and are willing to adjust tactics. Note a parallel in Trump's war in Iran. Iran uses inexpensive, quick to produce drones to attack targets; the US used old-school costly missiles which take over a year to produce.

Trump has rapidly depleted much of the US stockpile of Patriot missiles. The US has resorted to using inexpensive bombs. But history (Iraq War, War in Afghanistan, Gulf War, Vietnam War, Korean War, WWII) tells us bombing without an invading army won't win wars; even with an invading army wars can be lost.

Putin doesn’t care that Russia suffers human losses greater than Ukraine but he knows he is not winning his war. Similarly Trump doesn’t care that Americans suffer increasing costs of living due to his war but unlike Putin, Trump doesn’t know/understand/comprehend that bombing Iran will not win his war.

The US lacks/needs a patriotic cabinet member like minister Fedorov to tell him he is doomed to be the loser of his war with Iran.

comments.name: Blueandgreen802
comments.body: Reading this, I very much hope Zelensky changes his mind and reverses his decision. Bravo Fedorov for having the courage to speak truth to the military power structure and not go quietly. I cannot imagine how frustrating this is for the Ukrainian people when the war finally seem to be turning more toward Ukraine's favor. It also made me think of our Congress where the ancient politicians are gripping their power and privilege with their skeletal old hands. Come on, already. Embrace young leaders. Our vaunted Founding Fathers were, for the most part, YOUNG men. This whole world needs to shift to younger leadership. These are the people who will be living with the decisions made today for the next 30-40 years. They should be making the decisions that will affect them.

comments.name: drebt
comments.body: There is little disagreement that the drone tactics work. What this article does not tell us is if there was a disagreement over strategy, not tactics. Does Ukraine use drones against Russian troops in the Donbas, or do they use them against Russian infrastructure which supports and supplies those troops? This same question of strategy is as old as warfare itself. Ultimately armed forces need to occupy land for military success.  Perhaps that ugly fact was the motivation for President Zelensky's decision.

comments.name: Potter
comments.body:
Ukraine is a democracy. It's difficult to battle an attacking enemy  outside that is threatening your existence and at the same time keep a democracy within going. We must realize this. 
It's even more difficult when the enemy IS the leader and his minions, as in Putin's Russia, and increasingly, alas, here. 
Do the people hunker down as in Russia? or do they get louder.  
I have confidence that Ukrainians will come to resolving this split.They have to. We look to them, their spirit, now as we undergo a, urgent battle here our own democracy, a battle to keep our democracy. This is about us. Glory to Ukraine. And may our experiment that has inspired so many, survive our own split.

comments.name: John C
comments.body:
Burnham faces the same problem his immediate predecessors have. A public treasury drowning in debt, a country groaning under one of the heaviest tax burdens in the developed world, and a parliamentary backbench that has made it clear that whatever is to be done must not include any meaningful spending cuts. On top of this he is inheriting a national defense that has been so starved for money that there are more admirals in the Royal Navy than combat effective ships. Depending on what you count, Britain spends between seven and ten times as much on public welfare as it does on defense. In fairness, the Tories did little to deal with the insane government deficits they inherited from the Blair/Brown era during their long and often chaotic tenure in government.

Someone tasked with cleaning up Labour's mess at the end of the 1970s once noted "the problem with socialism, is that sooner or later you run out of other people's money to spend." That is still true today.

comments.name: Ned
comments.body: The author’s healthy dose of contempt for the British political class seems justifiable. “More of the same” seems to me as the only possible way.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: The UK should petition back into the EU; their “go it alone” philosophy has brought them this economic and social disaster.

comments.name: Jack Drinkem
comments.body:
We should remember that, pared down, governments were created to meet the needs of the people, not the wants of the people.  We need a safe environment to live in.  We need sufficient food to feed the people.  We need laws to protect the people.  We need some hope for the future, or why keep on living?

So, the real question that needs to be asked is: is the government, either ours or the Brits, providing this?  And, I would say that both countries have had recent governments that have centered on the wants, not needs.  Politicians can always play to the wants, but the society falters if the needs are not met.  So, the big question is will the new leader of Britain provide what the people actually need, not what they want?

Populists deliver what the people want.  Here in America, that seems to be too many spectacles, not what is necessary.   Do we really need to spend money on putting a cage up on the White House lawn for people to beat up other people?  Do we need a President who makes billions through graft?

I do not know what the British people actually need at this time.  But I hope they get someone who meets their needs far more than their wants, unlike our “leader”.

comments.name: Pete
comments.body:
The island kingdom has some intractable and structural economic problems that are not fixable.  Resources are scarce, and the cheap labor shifted from ag to industrialization in centuries past faces competition from nations emerging from poverty.

Empire was a temporary solution, based on ruling the seas in the days of sail and a mobile colonial army.  Gone, but the expectations and the futile and counterproductive strategies of the wealthy to cling to power still remain.

Cheap immigrant labor and the international banking and financing sector - crippled by Brexit and a febrile popular discontent looking for scapegoats.

There are no scapegoats, there is only a hard economic reality that the British public are unwilling to face.  Leadership changes are meaningless.

comments.name: TL
comments.body:
I am not British and have little idea of what Burnham will do -- or has done, for that matter.

But I do know that Hazeldine comes with his own (apparently hard-left) baggage and seems to have never forgiven Burnham for his rise during Blair's administration. Which can remind me of how *I* felt about some of the Clinton people during Bill's administration.

Well, for all of my disagreements with Clinton and his triangulation, I still admire his intelligence and political instincts, so I'm more forgiving of Burnham for now. If Burnham has failed to learn from the past, then Hazeldine can enjoy his slagging. If not, I hope he eats some crow.

comments.name: Papaya
comments.body:
I am hopeful for this prime minister. 

Small example: while on vacation listening to BBC4 in the car we heard about how Burnham wants to bring the process of buying a house in the US to the UK (which I have unfortunately experienced). There you require no earnest money, both sides can walk away at any time-gazumping, few ethical standards for brokers, no title insurance. It takes an age, even for an all-cash purchase and you might not secure the house you want after months of paperwork and thinking you have a deal. 

Things like these show that he is thinking how improving the process can help the country economically. I’m a fan so far.

comments.name: j b g
comments.body:
Hazeldine writes "from London."  Where else would a privileged voice damning Burnham's chances of improving life in Britain come from? The dominant right-wing media there are bent on destroying the country's best hope at present, after a Tory decade of incompetence, and Starmer's too-slow effort to mend the damage. Hazeldine at no point offers a convincing alternative.  So typical.
This is exactly what the next Democratic president faces here in the US - blame for wreckage that their party never caused.  And that will take a decade to repair.

comments.body: I'm not sure why every conversion is suspect because of one engineering failure.  Is this really a systemic issue?

comments.name: Diana M
comments.body: The solution is clear do not add floors to an existing structure case closed

comments.name: ROGER ROTHENBERGER
comments.body: There is no such thing as "pushing limits with architects and engineers". The codes are clear what needs to be done with any alteration either by design or construction sequence. Disclosure I am a registered professional civil engineer in California and New York.

comments.name: Rick C
comments.body:
"It is being investigated by the city,"  Uh oh.

The CE prof is correct. This is certainly not a turnkey design update.  Presumably a qualified A&E with a qualified structural analysis house did the design work. Even so to some degree this is plowing new ground.  Loads and margins need to be reviewed.  Also, don't assume just because a structural analysis showed adequate margin that the construction company and their subs followed their work instructions, used the correct materials, etc.  Where was the city with their inspections during the process?

comments.name: F S WOOD
comments.body: Seems crazy to allow developers to take the carved out interior space and add it on the roof - the building wasn't structurally engineered for those heights (which is the point of the article). My point is, NYC is due something a bit stronger than Hurricane Sandy and I wouldn't want to be in one of the rehabs.

"...The episode, (Berman) said, should be viewed as a construction problem that “has zero to do with the conversion...".

Interesting statement considering the construction is directly tied to the conversion.

comments.name: E Hines
comments.body:
It's more than just an inspection of the columns. The building's weight is delivered into the ground on which it sits. The foundation and foundation footings also need to be plussed up, the footings likely deepened further into the ground.

The nature of the ground complicates that, since the ground (not necessarily in the present case, but in general) can vary from locale to locale from an area that used to be boggy before urbanization to bedrock lying close to the surface.

Eric Hines

comments.name: Matthew F
comments.body: Just another New York conman…The episode, he said, should be viewed as a construction problem that “has zero to do with the conversion.” A buckled support beam because you’ve added floor space to an office building literally is the conversion.

comments.name: Red O. Greene
comments.body: From a chaplain and a physician, really excellent advice and suggestions.

comments.name: Westchester Peach
comments.body: I especially appreciate the verbal scripts Dr. Lori provides in her responses to these painful submissions. I would imagine telling your ailing spouse/business partner “I can’t do this without you” might put pressure on them, adding to the pain of their illness. Great to have her perspective and gentle neutrality we can all learn from. I hope LW feels supported and seeks guidance.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body: The last night of my mother's terminal illness, my brother arrived and so the entire family was together at bedside in the hospital. But reality was not discussed. Mom came outr of her light coma long enough to ask "What's happening? I don't want to die." But Mom was dying and I knew it. As the youngest, stay at home son, and as much a caregiver as her husband,  I knew enough about death to see it approaching. So Mom was given some pablum response by her husband and eldest child and I stayed silent; the doctors of the 1970s wouldn't say the truth to my other family members, so why should I?  After Mom died that night/early morning, everyone was  "surprised" except me. I had prayed that her suffering would end. My prayer was answered. But the fact that an opportunity to have a  final conversation about reality was lost to eternity, and the damage to the survivors was endless. Fifty years ago next April. My eldest sibling is now in memory care unable to recall anything specific about that experience. Dad remarried almost immediately back in the 1970s in a rebound attempt to bring Mom back; a nice person that   he soon regretted and admitted to me   that divorce might be necessary. Me, I went into therapy to spill my guts.

comments.name: Mark in Canada
comments.body: I have litigated "end of life" disputes - between treatment teams and families, and within families.  Most result from a failure to have had the conversations that capably convey wishes, values and beliefs.  That litigation leaves more damage, more scars, more regret and recrimination than any conversation about 'what to do when..' ever generated.  For the love of the people you love, HAVE THAT CONVERSATION WHILE YOU CAN!

comments.name: RC
comments.body: In the coming years astronomers will likely discover vast numbers of exoplanets with conditions close to those of Earth, yet missing the exact setups that have favored life on Earth. We could go on for years finding near-miss after near-miss. And that will underscore how unique our circumstances have been.

comments.name: 2Cents
comments.body: Finally a story that does not leave me in a state of despair!  What an achievement to make this discoveries. It gives me hope that there are people out there striving for knowledge and wonder.  Thank you to those that fund them, and thank you for telling us about it.

comments.name: Jupiter
comments.body:
I wonder how differently microscopic life would evolve on a planet that does not spin on its axis and has a 25‑day orbit around its star, compared to what we have observed on Earth.

I appreciate the author who imo, does a good job of breaking Terran-centric thinking. 
 
We assume that life needs the conditions we know. For years, science was hyper-fixated on oxygen atmospheres. A helium atmosphere changes everything… thermal dynamics, radiation shielding, and the way energy flows through the environment. What would life look like on a world where the sun never sets and never rises? What would it mean to adapt to a 25‑day year?

The discovery itself is remarkable, but what I find more interesting is how it forces us to recalibrate what we think life needs.

comments.name: Buja
comments.body:
Do we really have to be excited about this discovery? A few prominent scientists on Earth have already buried the idea of developing human civilization on our neighbour, Mars. 
Here we are discussing the possibility of an atmosphere eventually suitable for our life, but at a distance of a few light-years!
Sorry... this may be an exciting story for our scientists, but that's it.

articles.title: Less Is More in Higher Education
articles.summary: A bachelor’s degree in three years would cut costs and curb waste.

comments.name: steve cohen
comments.body: Also consider avoiding the large universities with their enormous tuition and fees, and look at smaller local options.  It is a terrible idea to enter the working world with crushing debt it takes many years to pay off.

comments.name: will mcgregor
comments.body:
As a parent of two college students, it was extremely frustrating paying tuition for useless electives. My kids thought it was stupid too as they would rather take another class in their major/ minor, work in a lab, take a part time job or work an internship.

More emphasis must be placed on real world job training skills and how to apply and be accepted into a good job.

comments.name: Kathleen Packard
comments.body: I teach concurrent enrollment (about $750 for 9 college credits) and AP chemistry ($100 for the exam) in a local public high school. I have found that few universities give credit for general chemistry courses for AP unless the student earns a 4 or 5 on the exam (although they do give elective credit). Concurrent enrollment generally will give them credit for a full year of gen chem 1 and 2 and lab, as long as they attend a public university.  However, this is getting more and more difficult for students to get credit for concurrent enrollment; it tells me that universities would not want to limit the time spent on tuition (and all the other stuff added to the bill) to 3 years.

comments.name: Rick Maybury
comments.body:
A bachelor's degree theoretically has to main goals: 

1. teaching people how to think, not what to think.  Engaging students in multiple disciplines to create the beginnings of a critical and analytical thinker, on the road to build judgment.  

 2. Giving students practical knowledge and skills to begin a productive career.

The challenge with a three-year degree is that a Bachelor's degree becomes more like a trade school degree, with an over focus on practical skills many of which will often be outdated before they even get to their first job.

Philosophically a BA degree should be teaching students how to think, how to learn and become life-long self-directed learners, and foundational practical skills since the will have to learn and adapt regardless of their first job opportunity.  

Our colleges have lost their way in terms of curriculum and purpose.  I think reducing the years is an efficiency solution to what is truly an effectiveness problem.

comments.name: David Williams
comments.body: How about eliminating any course or degree that ends in “studies”?

comments.name: David Moelling
comments.body:
I did a 4 year nuclear engineering Beng in 3.5 years in the 1970s with a couple of AP credits and a higher course load each semester.   You can do it in the existing system but need to have a planned required course schedule, and a good idea where you want to go.

Also avoid the "semester abroad" scam like the plague.  Unless there is a particularly good offering in your field you are just making money for your USA university, missing certain required courses and otherwise breaking an optimum sequence of courses to get you out early.

When we both retired again we had our 5100 sq. ft. custom home with a 6 car garage built for us on 40 acre of prairie in WY.  Six car garage is a bit a misnomer: tractor, tractor attachments, utility trailer, older pickup, SUV, and wife's road trip car.

comments.name: Independent
comments.body: Whenever I am asked where I am from, I tell them I am an Earthling.  I explain, an Earthling is one who travels, lives, works in different countries, adopting different languages and adapting to other peoples' cultural rituals.  "Do, as Romans do.", kind of attitude.  I  feel comfortable in my own skin, just about anywhere.  Jingoism is not my thing; people have different ways of doing things, but in the end, they all have the same aspirations and anxieties.  The place we are born is just a point on Earth, insignificant when we look at the Universe. Identifying  oneself as  American, Chilean or Canadian is just  for bureaucratic purposes, not a measure of one's worth nor that of the spot where we happened to be born.  Being  American-born or by choice, has a different meaning, of course.  It is a cultural "sheen" we all acquire in expression and manner that comes with time and exposure.  It is the brash and confident way we conduct ourselves in private and public that makes us stand out.  It is our constant desire to inquire, discover, solve and conquer problems.  That all spells: USA.  We are a dynamic cluster of people making good and bad things happen. We are a nation of immigrants; a nation of Earthlings bumping into each other finding out that we all are more alike than different.  I consider Stephen Miller, an aberration of our times, not someone I would have a beer with and say, "Salud", "Skol", "Cheers"!

comments.body: Two years ago I visited Athens, Greece and was atop the Parthenon and engaged a young 20 something Iranian woman in conversation.  She said she was unmarried and lived with her parents, and though she could leave the country for vacation, her parents had to stay as "hostages" (my word) and vice-versa.  I recommended Azar Nafisi's book to her, Reading Lolita in Teheran, and she asked me to enter the title and author into her iPhone—I asked whether that was safe for her, but she assured me that "it's not like that anymore."  Later I reflected how on my previous travels c1971, it was Greece that was under military rule (even dug up a photo I took of the Colonels in Syntagma square) and was able to (and did) travel anywhere in the Shah's Iran.  Perhaps then here's hope then for Iran, but sixty years is a long time to hold your breath.

comments.body: Trump wants to take is back further than the 1950's.  He wants to go all the way back to the 1890's, when William McKinley was President and made us an imperial power against everything that America's founders stood for.  His war of conquest of the Philippines netted us years of a bloody insurrection in those islands.  His tariffs to protect American industry and raise revenue which funded the government prior to the 16th Amendment which gave us the income tax is well documented.  It was the era of Plessy v Ferguson which created the racial doctrine of separate and equal and gave rise to Jim Crow law nationwide.   All of this should sound very familiar because Trump has duplicated it.  Those who do not learn from history repeat its mistakes and our failures.  As we continue to undermine American history in our education systems and in our national history museum at the Smithsonian w4e weaken civic understanding of exactly what American has been all about.

I have a kid (who is awesome) and it’s still hard every single day. My cat, however, is my unwavering emotional support in dealing with the rest of my family. I’m fact, he’s on my lap right now.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body:
I'm with her.  I am 70 and I never had children and very happy with my choice.  This doesn't mean I dislike children, in fact I enjoy time spent with my friends and meeting their grandchildren.
My joke:  I like with Karl Marx's brother Groucho had to say:  "Children are the opiate of the people."

comments.name: Jane Pratt
comments.body: I can relate to her frustrations as a childless woman.  My husband and I decided early in our marriage kids were not something we wanted. As I have gotten older, I do understand the natural conversational norm in our culture of asking women if they have kids, what they do for work, do they have a partner? But there are still a lot of people that react with shock when I say we didn't WANT kids, not that we couldn't have them. Considering that women still are battling for autonomy over our reproductive rights in this country and beyond, this type of rigid thinking about fertility is one and the same with the same patriarchal mindset of SCOTUS.

comments.name: f robertson
comments.body: I knew from an early age that children were not for me. I've never regretted my choice. I love kids and delight in my friend's offspring and I love the sound of my neighbor's grandchildren shrieking in delight, but nevertheless...

comments.name: Paula
comments.body:
I never wanted children.  Maybe my fraught relationship with mother had something to do with that, or not.  I wouldn't say I don't like children, but I honestly don't know how to relate to them, and when some friends made their children the very center of every social occasion, it was alienating.  

Maybe because highly educated career-oriented women of my generation (born in the 1950's) had to struggle exhaustively for inclusion, acceptance & promotion in many male-dominated schools & workplaces, there was less energy to think about whether or not to to have children. My parents did not push for grandchildren & in my friend circles I never felt judged for my choice, or my husband's, to not have chldren.

comments.name: KiruDub
comments.body:
My wife and I decided to not have children when we married back in 2001. I grew up in Africa (patents worked for UNICEF), so I saw first hand how overpopulated the developing countries are, and how grim the outlook for their youths. 

There are too many people on the earth already, and the reality is that having kids in the US is *expensive*.

Now we go to restaurants and see families with the parents completely tuned out, staring at their phones, with the kids either doing the same thing or wailing on each other to keep busy. 

And a friend with teen-aged kids talks about how stressed & depressed they are about their futures... so nope, I think we dodged a bullet given the timeline we're in right now.

A child born in 2026 will almost definitely have a harder life than its parents. Poorer, less stable, probably less free. Refusing to bring new life into this disaster is a mercy.

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
The irony is that in many ways, Burnham is a vestige of the past.  His position as "King of the North" speaks to the fact that England's northwest, together with neighboring Scotland, were bulwarks of the Labour Party.

But Scotland is no longer a region likely to once again become the Labour stronghold it once was.

And Burnham's own region has now swung over to the right and the King's crown there now lies on Nick Farage's head.

Simply put, Britain is likely undergoing a major political realignment.  One that led first to Brexit and now appears likely to disrupt not just Labour, but the Tories as well.

When Britain was an EU member the Tory stronghold in southeast England prospered and grew.  It embraced EU membership and its geographical position tied it more to the Continent than to the rest of the UK.

But at the same time, the north of England, particularly the once industrial powerful northeast, continued to economically decline.  It's aging industrial base was decaying and it's remoteness from the Continent made revival all but impossible.

It was the northwest that became a Brexit stronghold and, perhaps ignored at the time, signaled the decline of the Labour Party.

If you look at Burnham's plans -- they revolve around trying to revive a moribund industrial northwest of England by continuing a policy of "apartness" from Europe.  A policy so contrary to the interests of the southeast.

Burnham won't "unite" Britain -- he'll deepen its divisions.

comments.name: NYT Reader
comments.body:
I’m going to be wildly contrarian on the “social” aspect. It is great for live concerts, for sure. Or sports events. Feeling like part of an army, a militia, all souls in  a choir of a common anthem. 

 But for a movie, no, there is no socializing going on. You’re quietly (I would hope) watching a movie by yourself and soaking in the director’s vision, the themes of the writers, the subtlety of the actors, the lush cinematography and enchanting score, etc.

Other people in the theater can only ruin that and take you out of the experience. Gross smelly, nauseating fake buttered popcorn. People shuffling into their seats after it started, blocking your view, taking your seat because assigned seating is a stupid system and people naturally want to sit where they feel like when they get there; talking during the movie, controlling rowdy children

Yeah, no thanks. I like theaters for superior sound and picture and the feeling of being able to say I saw it live when it came out. Not because of but in spite of the others in the theater.

The social aspect is not in viewing but in discussing it after the fact with friends and family, being a shared cultural thing to discuss. TV can’t be that anymore because people watch stuff of any different era. But new movies and sports are still water cooler material.

I go sometimes three times a week. I almost exclusively support indie films or "smart" films or films outside the hollywood formula. I prioritize suppoting our one independent theater with one screen here.  I loved Obsession and Back Rooms as a 62 year old btw. When I go on Tues and Wed the movie is only $6 at AMC. I almost always splurge on popcorn and water even though the water is $6. I do that to support the theater financially. I don't want them to close. I also get points so I am really not paying that full price. Because I tend to go to the smarter movies or movies on tues and wed afternoon the crowds are often better "behaved" and often on a Tuesday afternoon I am the youngest person there at 62!

It is good to finally see Zoomers coming out, I too thoroughly enjoyed ‘Obssession,’ and was delighted how a young filmmaker could show Hollywood that you don’t need the $250 million production to have a hit. My kids are both 20 and we hung out last night. I was struck by how intensely they were interested in going to the movies this summer.

Old movies, new movies, often in theaters, sometimes on small screens watching in groups of four or eight. They see the new trending movies. They watch Kiarostami movies, “old” movies from the early 2000s and before, “Trainspotting,” “Stalker,” “Nashville” and on and on. (They have their doubts about “The Odyssey,” though.)

I can’t say how widespread this trend is, with my tiny anecdotal sample size. But it’s not just these two young people. 

My daughter saw “The Third Man” at Film Forum this summer and loved it, and then my son saw it there and loved it, and then their close friend in Massachusetts was eager to see it too. He loved it.

There is still motivation among some kids to get into movies. There are many young cinephiles out there.

comments.name: hen3ry
comments.body:
This is why research funds should not be made into political weapons.  The only woke thing that belongs in judging a grant worthy of funding is its merit based upon the science.  There are other horrible diseases out there that kill people.  Some occur solely in certain populations.  Sickle cell anemia is one.  Cystic fibrosis is another.  This cancer seems to prefer children or young adults.  Some illnesses occur almost exclusively in one sex:  hemophilia, muscular dystrophy, prostate cancer.  

Cures are built on small steps.  One step might help in concert with another to prevent this cancer from progressing too rapidly.  Another part of the cure might be found in an obscure fungus or a snail.  Researchers don't know and they, and the patients, especially the patients, deserve a chance to contribute to finding a cure.  

The only reason some of us are alive today is because of research that came to fruition for our parents or our grandparents.  That research may have involved public health, vaccines, antibiotics, insulin, or something else.  At some point some of these fatal conditions will stop being fatal and move to chronic or curable.  Research is the way to make this possible. 

I hope that at some point no parent has to watch their child die.  Parents do not expect to outlive their children.

comments.name: P k
comments.body:
“But last year was supposed to be the hundred-year flood. This is unexpected.”

Well, as more and more fossil fuels are burned (to the tune of a 100 billion barrels of oil every single day), CO2 concentration in Earth's atmosphere increases, and every year sets a new record high in atmospheric CO2 concentrations!

As CO2 concentration increases, Earth's average temperature increases (as does ocean temperature).

And most importantly in this situation: for every one degree Celsius rise in temperature in Earth’s atmosphere, 

the amount of water vapor the atmosphere can hold increases by about 7%!
(from Clausius–Clapeyron relation in thermodynamics). 

This means that a parcel of air can suck up more moisture (and if not released right away) causes droughts; 

or, 
if atmospheric forcing causes a sudden release of that water vapor: 
major flooding!
(like this current event, and the July 2025 Texas floods that killed a bunch of children). 

In addition: as ocean temperatures rise, evaporation increases, and any "atmospheric river" flooding events that form become more intense.

Just look at how CO2 has risen over time:

year: CO2 concentration (mean)

comments.name: Look Ahead

A person interviewed for a different article said she couldn’t afford to buy a house so she was going on an expensive vacation instead.

My initial reaction was judgmental. My second reaction was, “wait, that was us!”. Except we went one better by quitting our jobs during the Great Recession of 1981 to travel. And then again in 1983. And then we had kids. By the 1990s we were deep in the hole. But we bought our first house in the mid-1990s, and with frugality, we eventually managed to retire. 

And while we love our home, I’m not sure home ownership is the best for everyone. In the past year, we needed a new roof, furnace, dishwasher and major tree service, in addition to all of those other unplanned expenses like car repairs and dentist bills. 

We inherited almost nothing from our hard working parents because they grew up in the pension generation, before 401ks, which actually create intergenerational wealth without all of the burdens of home ownership.

What it doesn't understand is that tech does not need Europe.  Country just provides an environment.  Tech simply seeks the best environment for it to evolve.  Tech doesn't even depend on human being.  It picked human as its carrier in a sense, because we were best fit its evolvement.  If someday, this no longer be true, tech will move to a different carrier, and we will end up the losers of tech evolution, like all other animals existed or still existing on this planet.

comments.body: Europeans always have delusions of grandeur before reality hits.  Remember the Euro replacing the dollar as the world reserve currency after the 2008 financial crisis?  This is more of the same.  There is no cohesive entity called Europe.  It is made up of a mix of middle power and small states that do not have a shared fate or common destiny like the citizens of the United States or the Chinese subjects.  Look at how the the recent German - French jet plane project failed recently.  It's a microcosm of the inefficiencies in Europe, which has left the continent in the past and displaced by China as a geopolitical power.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Ultimately, it's not the country that is important.  It's the person controlling the tech that is important.  Once AGI and physical AI become reality, traditional services, such as security and justice, provided by states become obsolete.  Physical constraints also become irrelevant.  Those controlling tech can deployed unlimited capacity in and obtain unlimited resources and energy from the outer space.  AI will predict and analyze problems and provide solutions.  Robots will provide goods and services, enforce justices, and provide security.  Individuals mastering will become sovereign, because they can defend themselves from anything the society wants impose on them. Would it matter which countries those individuals come from?  I don't think so, because they are sovereign.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Quest for tech sovereignty is not hard.  In fact, there are only a handful of simple rules to follow.  First is a brutal work ethics.  Think about how Elon and his fellow entrepreneurs work. Second is deregulated environment where people are encouraged to innovate and set up new businesses.  More rockets are now launched for private business use than NASA projects.  Third, a unified market where innovations can be deployed quickly, instead of facing fragmented political and regulatory environment.  China and the US check all 3 boxes. Europe checks none.  It's not the task that is difficult.  It's a choice of the wrong social paths.

Competition leads to creativity and innovation so are absolutely essential for any economy. A reality so many do not want to accept or adapt to. 

In a few stronger places like Switzerland and Norway governments actually support businesses & innovation with temporary tax breaks for start ups etc.  - who else create jobs? A frightening portion of EU  citizens mostly want earlier retirement, more vacations and shorter workweeks + gov subsidies to pay for their needs. 

In Europe those needed business choices are hampered at every turn by gov/political/"expert" "regulations" & unions that have far more to do with distributing to the "their bases", protecting jobs beyond their sell or knowledge dates ....  than the progress of society and nation for future generations.  

Government and union employees have their own interests at heart, first and foremost in most countries.

I understand that he is personally frustrated by the decision to cut him loose but public whining while his country is in a fight for its survival is selfish and irresponsible.

Perhaps Zelensky had other problems with this obviously talented but also apparently self absorbed young man.  I would frankly trust Zelensky’s judgement given what he has done since this war started.

I am impressed with what I have read but his stint in Defense is relatively short lived and Ukraine has been innovative in technology since the outset of the conflict.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
Kudos to younger adults in Ukraine for innovation and independent thinking. But it does not logically follow that only young adults can save Ukraine and that anyone over 30 is a jaded, incompetent hack. That is pure ageism, and any blanket disregard for the thoughts of experienced military officers is a mistake. Personnel decisions need to be driven by a nuanced consideratiion of diverse facts and performance, not cultural tropes. And if Fedorov had some relationship issues with some generals, and if these issues were interfering with his running the ministry of defense, it makes no sense to overgeneralize that the generals must be wrong just because thay are older than Fedorov. And there is no concrete 'old vs young,'- there is just older and younger. Hegseth is young- you trust him?

This is a perfect opportunity for Russian intelligence to use its social media intervention machine to drive division within Ukraine. They amplify any social discord within any society to destroy it. Just like they still do every day against the United States. And these rather one-sided news stories just perpetrate that in the search for more readership and likes, just like they are pitting the young versus old in the US. Well, divided we fall...

comments.body:
I get the impression that Ukraine struggling through a major generational (r)evolution that can't come soon enough to America: out with the old (like me! I'm 72) and in with the new. in with those who will live with choices made today.

There is a highly resistant old guard, too accustomed to power and to "tradition", which is just another way to say "I'm the boss, I know the way things should be, I won't change."

It can't come soon enough.

comments.name: Nathan Kerr
comments.body:
Whomever was in charge of this up to the CEO should get a Red Card. IMMEDIATELY. Most Americans do not watch or care about soccer for 3+ years. Then the world's largest tournament comes to these shores and you can't get a replica jersey? I mean even TikTok of Private Airline Concierge services were looking high and low for these things for its clients. No dice. If those that spend tens of thousands of dollars to fly a few hundred miles can't get one I mean you have messed up.

I wanted one as I attended a watch party at UBS Arena vs Australia. None were available. Face it, they are making these in China where labor costs are like a dime a day per worker. They should have stocked up and if there were extras sell them 50% off once the US was eliminated. You still would make a profit. The home jersey(which I didn't like) would have been great for the 4th of July anyway.

comments.name: Srdjan Knezevic
comments.body:
It's articles like this that make it easier to subscribe to WSJ.  I really like the crossover of business and sport and culture here.

From Canada (Serbian background) can say the World Cup in the US was a success, the Americans met the moment and were great hosts.  The team performed so well until undone by the controversy around the red card reversal/suspension.

The US Nike jerseys were a total hit and Nike missed in not ordering more of the US and France jerseys.  The authentics are worth it and make great collector items  for years to come and for the next World Cup (notice some of the USA '94 type of detailing on releases by both Nike and adidas for all national teams apparel like the adidas EQT line).

The article should point out the amount of discounting adidas has to do because of sponsoring or over-ordering for maybe too many national teams.

I would like to note that it is not like On is a competitor on the soccer front. And their stock hasn't exactly been performing like a memory chip company...  Nike has understandably focused on catching up in the running race.  I do hope that the World Cup makes them more soccer focused. 

Would like to see Nike limit the amount of "signature shoes" for basketball players, seems like those are way over-ordered and over-stocked and destined for sales racks.

Every time I fill my petrol tank and watch the dollars zoom up, I think of Trump and the war America started in the Middle East.
Every time I buy an item like a refrigerator or a TV set, I marvel at how much more affordable these items are compared to when I was younger. Nearly every item in my house comes from China.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body:
One day global climate disasters will really, really start to become the norm, rather than a surprising exception. About midway through the 20th century the US was responsible for 40% of the cumulative CO2 emissions for the entirety of human history. That’s bad enough, but worse is that we used the immense economic advantage gained from all that combustion not to build renewable energy systems, but to steal and burn more fossil fuels through violence, deception, and privatized profits while everyone else deals with the costs. The global hegemony being anti-science won’t last, and the eventual invoice for all the damage is going to be immense. A recent study put it at $10 trillion, with $4 trillion self-inflicted. 

Trump uses billions in taxpayer funds to stop wind power plants and prop up coal instead, then bombs Iran to and starves Cuba for not letting western companies ransack their resources. Meanwhile, China builds a GW of solar every 8 hours. 

If these mid-terms get effectively cancelled due to ICE at swing state poll sites we are in for an even worse second half of this term and beyond. 2027 will be the hottest year on record due to El Niño and the lawless data center expansion while suppressing new power plants in the name of being anti-woke will eventually lead to catastrophic heatwave blackouts. On climate and the future, China makes the US look intentionally incompetent to the point of genuine stupidity. It’s going to cost us way more than the stock market.

comments.name: Someone
comments.body: That may be true, but my 40 year living in this country, I never see such negative opinions towards China. More I never see China is such diplomatic isolation around its neighbors. With its one way trade policy, China has trade frictions not only with US but also with Eurozone and other countries. For sure China actually progresses in many areas are not carefully studied by Western and US intellectual circles. Instead we keep pointing out its political system weaknesses.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
It is not a coincidence, surprise, or that China suddenly changed itself. China is simply being itself, and today’s geopolitics has offered the world an opportunity to understand China better, with less filtered glasses.

Yes, China still has many problems, both domestically and internationally. But this period is also a wake-up call, particularly for some Western-aligned perspectives that may have underestimated or misunderstood China’s trajectory.

A civilization that has existed for 5,000 years is still, in many ways, misunderstood by many in the West. Western countries may still not like China, and that is their choice. But at least this moment has offered a chance to see China more clearly and understand it beyond existing narratives.

Zero intrinsic value tokens, like bitcoin, doge, trump, melania, and literally thousands of other such tokens, are all objectively worth zero real money. They are thin air, just like the tokens of the monopoly game you have in your cabinet.

Yet amazingly, there seems to be a difference in the price of thin air. The reason is obviously the amount of hype such a token gets from influencers. And yet, tokens can have a real value, if a company can guarantee that it is backed by real assets. I guess more and more people are waking up to the difference.

Being able to go long or short on bitcoin means that nowadays for a new beginner trying his luck, it is no longer the price that matters, but only the prediction of the direction. 

For people with a hoard of such tokens, it is obviously paramount that the price should go up, especially if you are under water. Many of that older crowd is on social media daily, telling each other how things must get better.

It is strange to see this entire article argued without reference to the continuing ambiguity of American possession of its own colonial territories… places like Puerto Rico and American Samoa, where inhabitants are Americans but without the full rights of American citizens.

comments.name: Strongbow
comments.body:
The author refers to European nations surrendering elements of their sovereignty when they join the European Union.

This is not the case, or no more the case than when a country freely enters into any international agreement. The European Union institutions have only delegated power from the national states. They have no autonomous powers of their own and no legal ability to acquire any such powers.

The European Union is a system of permanent and structured negotiation between the member states over certain limited  matters and includes mechanisms for making and enforcing decisions arising from such negotiations.

This involves the member states undertaking to abide by the rules they have agreed to and by the decisions made in accordance with those rules. It does not involve any member state according ceding sovereign power to any other member state or to autonomous European institutions.

This very sophisticated system is not only difficult for outsiders to understand: it is also difficult for many Europeans to comprehend. European populists love criticizing "Brussels" as if the European institutions were a foreign entity - and the Trump administration now provides official encouragement from the US for them to do so.

But when correctly understood, for any European, Brussels is not "them": it is really the reflection of a larger "us", the product of agreement as an antidote to confrontation and an essential condition of relevance in the world.

comments.name: John R. Ross
comments.body:
The restoration of Penn Station should not present significant complexities, particularly given the presence of shorter platforms.

It is my understanding that Mr. Andy Byford is primarily focused on optimizing through-run operations within Penn Station, especially considering that Amtrak largely originates its services from Sunnyside Yard and Boston. Establishing a comprehensive train station hub at Sunnyside Yard appears to be a viable option, particularly as Mayor Zohran Mamdani is exploring the utilization of air rights for development in that area.

Furthermore, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority is actively integrating Metro-North Railroad services into Penn Station through the Penn Access initiative. This development represents a continuation of historical patterns, as New Haven is once again sharing Penn Station, now with an expanded array of services.

The most feasible option to minimize dwell time and platform space for Long Island Rail Road trains is to create services on the West Side via Amtrak, including a new station at West 125th Street serving Columbia University, with an option for a 96th Street station as well.

These measures would ensure smoother operations at Penn Station.

I have confidence in Mr. Byford, and I believe he will deliver a truly transformative experience for travelers. I wish him the best of luck.

comments.name: john otoole
comments.body:
China’s Two-Speed Economy Pairs High-Tech Success With Domestic Gloom

I don't wield the economic education to compare China's economic strength with ours but, living in China 17 of the past 24 years and currently, I can critique comparative gloom.

Young Chinese of working age (of which I have 4000 former students in their 30s and early 40s - an anecdotal cohort to be sure, but a sizeable one) are certainly stressed, but their anxiety differs from my children's compatriots in several ways.

First, PRC citizens genuinely trust CPC governance.  Right or wrong, they see their future as improving under Xi and gang.

Second, each of them are only two generations, some three, from ancestors who literally died of hunger.   They didn't observe it, but the stories are ubiquitous.

Third, they are not barraged daily by a two-party system of politicians wailing on media of fraud, felony and failure.

Fourth, they are products of a culture which successfully propagandizes consensus, harmony and struggle.

I need not explain U.S. citizens to you.

comments.body: People do not die of pneumoonia unless they have a pre-existing health issue. In Sam Neil's case, his Cart T therapy for Lymphoma may have had a serious impact on his immune system, exposing him to the risk of sepsis which leads to death in immunocompromised patients. Leaving this info out does a disservice to your readers.

comments.name: GEW
comments.body:
Big fan of the new therapies for blood cancers… I have had a form of lymphoma for a long time and been kept alive with immunotherapy agents.  They are genuinely life extending and we are so lucky to live in an era where such therapies are available.

That said….

If Mr. Neal had Car-T therapy and died from pneumonia, it is more than likely that his therapy rendered him immunocompromised. It’s a known thing that these therapies work by ridding various blood cells that assist or even drive the immune system.

I just wish that it didn’t get swept under the rug. Hear me out.

When I was diagnosed, I was assured my particularly form of lymphoma was treatable and it would not kill me. That said, the longer I live with it, the more I understand that what will probably kill me is an infection like this one. Yet I am constantly having to ask friends to not come around me when ill because the danger of my immunocompromisation. They ask breathlessly about a cancer that won’t kill me all the while bringing coughs and ailments that actually really could. 

And while I am so grateful, it doesn’t render the thread of germ compolications any less. So when I have to bow out of things like trips to remote parts of the world, or have to weigh all fun decisions against the risk of catching something, it gets exhausting explaining over and over again.

It’s a conversation that needs to happen. These drugs are miracles, but the risks are real.

comments.name: North Carolina
comments.body: One of the consequences of cancer treatment is that the treatment can leave you weak and susceptible to infection or damage to other critical functions that can not be treated due to the condition of the patient. Neill's t-cell treatment might have left him susceptible to infection and made pneumonia treatment harder. Wish he had gotten his extra decade or two.

comments.body: It is a pity the photo with Babitz was not included by the MoMA to add context. Or did I miss it despite going four times? Other great contemporaries of Duchamp, including his theoretical antagonist Picasso, have been photographed with nude women, and the motivations can be difrent in each case, and not always documented. It is possible to speculate about sexism in the photo, with the anachronism this may imply, but it is also possible to speculate that Duchamp was illustrating how a chess game can be so engrossing as to eliminate other distractions. As an analogy, there are those of us who have dogs and amaze our friends when we genuinely focus on the dogs we meet and not their attractive owners. I think I get Duchamp at that level :-)

comments.name: Dennis
comments.body: The belief that art cannot have constraints is widespread but fundamentally untrue. Constraints exist even in the choice of medium, the specs of the spaces the art can be shown, a patron's or client's requirements, etc, --and, in the end, the artist's ability or imagination. Some people believe anything can be art and some people don't. Both can be right. Genius is as much about what we can do within given or implicit constraints as with ignoring or challenging  them. In the end, what matters is whether what we have is good art or bad art. Intuitively, we respect artists who can execute with artisanal mastery, because there is a connection between art and craft. It is a valid but not necessary or sufficient criterion. What is important when we evaluate a work of art is to have multiple criteria, and, implicitly, we have. We do not all need to have the same criteria but we all need a solid and broad grounding in art history and frequent interaction with art really matters.

comments.name: Expat
comments.body:
For some reason, my previous comment about the photo of Duchamp and Babitz was not approved. I am trying again. 
There is more to the history of the photo. Babitz was having an affair with the owner of the gallery. (She was a famous paramour of many celebrities in her life, as noted in her obit in The Times: https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/19/obituaries/eve-babitz-dead.html). On opening night of the retrospective, she was not invited because the wife of the gallery owner would be there. Adding insult to injury, Babitz's sister was invited. She and Wasser hatched a scheme to get even and Duchamp went along with it. (In other words, it was not his idea.) They staged the photo in the gallery and timed it around the time the gallery owner usually arrived. When it did, he saw the scene and purportedly spit out the gum he was chewing. The whole story has been well documented and also appears in a book called Chess Players from Fuel Publishing, which includes many other photos, and histories, of famous people playing chess.

Any project involving Adani deserves careful scrutiny given the company's track record of environmental controversies.
For example, Adani's proposed Great Nicobar development project has drawn widespread criticism from environmental scientists and conservationists. They warn that it could destroy large areas of pristine rainforest, threaten endangered species such as the giant leatherback turtle, reduce biodiversity, and adversely affect Indigenous communities, including the Shompen and Nicobarese peoples.
India is also facing an increasingly severe water crisis. Summers in many regions are now routinely reaching temperatures of 45°C or higher. Hundreds of millions of people still lack access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation, while groundwater depletion, polluted rivers, and climate change are placing additional stress on already limited water resources.
At the same time, India is working to expand access to piped drinking water nationwide, making water conservation more critical than ever. This is one reason why many communities in the United States have also opposed large data center projects, citing concerns over their enormous water consumption, high energy demands, and pressure on local infrastructure and ecosystems.
Innovation and economic development are important, but they should not come at the expense of forests, biodiversity, Indigenous communities, or already scarce natural resources.

Education is a much bigger priority on average in the Asian Family dynamic, especially in a culture where children are seen as eventual care takers. The parents will often sacrifice almost everything to get their kid into an extra study program to enhance their kids viability as a candidate to enter a good high-school then college no matter how financially strapped they may be. Life isn't like a race track, no one starts on equal footing, and there is no simple solution to bringing more and much needed diversity into the best public education programs in the city. comments.name: Lee Boot
comments.body:
I taught at a prestigious independent school for eleven years, then at a public magnet school for six years. I live in Baltimore.

There is a form of context that matters, and as Mr. McWhorter frames it, it matters before the test. There is robust social psychology, with academic terms like “social learning theory” and “self‑efficacy,” that is best summed up by what marketing expert Seth Godin describes in seven words: “People like me do things like this.”

In other words, the history of behavior and consequent achievement that a young person understands about their family or community (true or not) will shape what they aim for because achieving it will allow them to meet the standard required for status in that social context. No one wants to be the family or neighborhood under achiever. Most will do what it takes, even if it is very hard, because that is social survival.

If a community is barred, as Black Americans were for generations, from participating in the best schools regardless of effort and achievement, other paths will become the social norm and set the socio‑cultural pattern. A young person must become a social eccentric to follow a different path once the bar is lifted. How many of us would be the one who does that?

Discussion of community norms—despite their external causes—is politically sensitive and should be, but we cannot move forward until we are honest. Success begets success, and culture is the strongest influence on discretionary behaviors.

comments.name: preiher

“But A.I., depending on how far and fast it progresses, poses a dilemma for the ruling Communist Party. How should it manage the rise of a technology that could one day be so disruptive that it could threaten its interests — and its grip on power?” 

Yes, these are early days, but I believe the possibility of A.I. being utilized to undermine the CCP, and offer Chinese citizens an opportunity to develop and build a “Democracy With Chinese Characteristics” is, though presently inchoate, rich in potential for what would certainly be the Premier Revolution and Event of the 21st Century. 

(If Vladimir Putin is still around, we can let him pick the “Color.”) 

Want a more peaceful World, with an increased level of broadly-defined security for the International Community, and its Citizens? 

Well, I guess the A.I.-Assisted possibilities to pursue are myriad. 

We often hear about the Dystopian scenarios … 

But, a much more positive future is also possible. And I look forward to a China, and its People, fully partaking in the fruits of those efforts. 

There’s so much to be written on that “Blank Paper.”

In a Starbucks in an outer suburb of Guangzhou this afternoon, I couldn't find a seat.   The place was packed with young professionals who, by their dress and age, should have been at a job on a weekday.

I asked my former student and lunch companion, who works evenings 'live streaming' on U.S. Facebook selling counterfeit handbags, about AI.

"It's cute and fun!"

Young Chinese are not connecting their employment struggles with AI, even as factory jobs disappear, replaced by robots, and large tech employers shed workers.  There is none of the anger at AI that fills media articles in the U.S.

The CPC is, as always, managing the media narrative.   There may be concern about AI in Zhongnanhai, but there is no pressure on the government to 'manage' AI risk being exerted by the population.

OpenAI’s greatest impact may not be on the balance of power between nations but on the balance of knowledge between elites and ordinary people. If AI makes education available to billions of people, the creative capacity could expand on a scale never witnessed. Thus, the right-framed question should not be whether America or China wins the AI race, but whether humanity wins the education race.

comments.name: wrcoll
comments.body:
There's a different kind of counting theorem for convex polyhedra: Euler's Polyhedra Formula. Count all the pentagons (faces F), all the line segments around the faces (Edges E) and all the points where edges meet (Vertices V) and Euler mostly proved the following formula:

V - E + F = 2

A soccer ball is just a slightly distorted polyhedra so it should work there. A banana is another example. It has two verticies (the two ends), five faces (most bananas have five segments going around, and matching five edges. Hence 2 - 5 + 5 =2. Same for an American football. Or a cube: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2.

The use of mathematical ideas and exceptional visuals to make sense of a common object (a soccer ball, or "football" as most of the world disturbingly calls it ;-) places math and formal ideas in their most accessible role: allowing us to explore the hidden possibilities and limits of the everyday world of objects that we take for granted as simpler than they are.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: Considerations of symmetry (or operations) are the sine qua non in modern physics. For example time symmetry (the assertion that the laws pf physics do not change over time) shows, through the Emmy Noether theorem, that energy in a closed system is conserved. As one other reader already stated, mathematical group theory and representation theory are at the heart of particle physics. Quarks were speculated to exist on the basis of representation theory by Murray Gell-Mann. Representation theory helps us understand an abstract mathematical group by mapping its elements to concrete symmetries or operations acting on a physical system, allowing us to analyze how that system transforms under the group's actions

I’m from Uruguay, we didn’t have MTV until 1994 ish. But I had friends living in NY, they just recorded 24 hours MTV  for me and l sent me the VHS.

120 minutes was by far my favourite show. I remember loving his accent and how knowledgeable and cool he was. 

Buen viaje Mr. Kendall, you made a huge impact on a little punk girl on the other side of the world.
