comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
I for one will lament the loss of the 160 year tradition of Horse Carriage Rides in Central Park. They are romantic, colorful reminders of Old New York and a lovely tourist attraction. Tourism is an essential contribution to the City's economic health. 

It is regrettable, but accidents happen. A tourist or anyone could be robbed or shot in Times Square or hit by a car or delivery bike. The City Council is not banning cars or deliveries or visiting Times Square.

I care deeply for the health and well being of the horses, but I find the opponents objections overblown and indignant. I also care for the well being of the Carriage Drivers. They have made many accommodations over the years, but now their livelihood and a wonderful New York tradition is being destroyed. It's the wrong thing for the City Council to impose.

comments.name: Calliegirl
comments.body:
My grandfather drove a horse carriage in NYC, after being chronically unemployed throughout the Great Depression. He loved his horses and took very good care of them. He took great pride in what he did, always dressed elegantly and wore a top hat. I think it was the best job he ever had. 

Although I do understand, I am sorry to see all the negative sentiment around this issue. Times change, I guess.

comments.name: frees
comments.body:
horses and other animals have been pulling wagons, carriages, logs, and other things for ages and most likely will continue to be used in such ways.  carriage rides are not unique to NYC.  that there have been incidents that get wide coverage is sad but sadly part of life for all of us.  accidents happen.  are bikes going to be banned because a bike rider was recently killed in an accident on a bridge? doubt it.
regulate the industry for safety sake but leave it be.

comments.name: Deborah Kent-Clark
comments.body: This is great news if indeed the horses are finally set free. None them look "happy." It is time to come into the 21st century by ending the carriage rides. Some other tourist attraction will most likely be created to replace it.

comments.name: Fitzman
comments.body: To ban the carriage horses would be like pulling down statues of controversial historic figures in an effort to try to erase history because you don't agree with its existence. Other cities in the US and around the world have similar carriage horse services with few issues, as an example take a look at Charleston S.C their horse carriage industry is highly regulated with few issues. Instead of a total ban right away, a compromise to restrict the industry to operation in central park only and increase regulation and licensing of the drivers and carriage owners may bring some control to the industry that currently has too many horses and carriages sharing the public streets with cars and trucks.

comments.name: Brookdale66

It’s tragic that a young man recently died when he was thrown from a carriage, but his family should not be demanding all carriages be removed. If he had fallen and hit his head while riding a bicycle would they be demanding that no one be allowed to ride a bike anymore?

First, there is an increased prevalence only in Midwestern states plus Kentucky. Second, no specific source has been identified so "word on the street" not only unscientific, but increases confusion and disseminate inaccurate information. Third, there is much much greater likelihood of contracting 
Norovirus or Campylobacter. An article that addressed this was very recently published in the New York Times. I'm not aware of any data suggesting water contamination in general in affected state and unlike produce, it would not be shipped from state to state. Lastly, the parasite and its eggs are not, I repeat not eradicated by washing. Only boiling destroys them.

I think that those who are taking precautions right now are wise, particularly if they are immunocompromised or elderly.  Getting sick for days or weeks can be truly depleting.  Even if people thoroughly wash the affected produce, it reduces risk, but doesn’t eliminate it.

With a 40 TRILLION in debt, another never ending war, huge amounts of the country in a severe drought, safety nets being ripped away, the thought of building 100's or 1000's of data centers is irresponsible.

comments.name: Michael Treleaven
comments.body: Quite rich of the Republicans to "blame Canada".  The GOP is the party of climate denial, and its leader has been trying to get coal burning energy facilities back online, has gutted climate science support, and caused the USA to exit global climate work.  Anxious to bring back the 1950s, the Republican Party escapes into its fantasies and attempts to shift blame to other Americans and other countries.  If and when the USA gets serious about the climate crisis, maybe then the GOP might be able to stare down the Canadians, the Europeans, the Australians, et alia.

comments.name: Lyn
comments.body: “If Canada will not manage its forests to prevent these fires, the United States will look elsewhere, and act on our own, to protect our people,” four Republican members of Congress from Michigan wrote in a letter to Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, on Wednesday.   The hypocrisy is staggering.

comments.name: garvie
comments.body: As a Canadian I'm really very sorry this is happening to all of us people on any side of the border and also to the forests and their inhabitants.

comments.name: Doyle Alexander
comments.body:
The threats directed at Canada are outrageous and a direct outcome of Trump's endless lies and venom which has trained his followers to hate their ally to the north.  

Everyone knows this is caused by climate change which has dried out the previously wet boreal forest. The scale is vast, larger than several states combined, in an area with no roads and no human habitation. It is not physically possible to "manage" these forests or the resulting fires; all that can be done is to protect communities.

When the US burns Canada sends waterbombers, not insults.  Do better, GOP.

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
Canadian boreal forests are massive, second in size only to Siberian. And, worse, both have been drying out for decades--as well as large portions of permafrost.

For Republican politicians to blithely admonish the Canadian government for not "managing" forests to prevent fires" is shameless nonsense.

It reminds of the blovatios, sepremely unqualified Wizard of Oz, hidden behind a curtain espousing nonsensical threats.

Similarly, many US southwest states are experiencing a decades long drought.

These events are driven by climate change; rising temperatures and reduced snowpack desicate soil and vegetation over large areas are turning these ecosystems into highly flammable tinder, fueling unprecedented, massive wildfires and accelerating the die-off of trees, especially at the southern portion of the ecosystems.

Moreover, plant hardiness zones are steadily shifting northward as average winter temperatures warm.

The science and data are irrefutable. There is no alternate scientific analysis backed by reems of data, modeling, and rigorously peer reviewed by experts in absolutely every field. Period.

comments.name: RBB
comments.body: The hubris and inability to see irony from these Republicans is amazing. Wildfire seasons are now longer and more intense  DUE TO CLIMATE DISRUPTION and all these politicians can do is bloviate and further alienate and harass Canada. As someone who loves our northern neighbors, please forgive us, our Canadian friends!

articles.title: When American Smoke Choked Canada
articles.summary: Some Republican lawmakers have blamed Canada for poor air quality in the United States and said poor forest management is to blame. But Canadians have also inhaled smoke from American wildfires.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body:
I was the same...not a soccer 'fan' or even a 'follower,' but having watched the matches, at this point, I 'know' the main players and have some idea of what is going on.

I'm looking forward to the weekend, although with smoke in NYC, I hope everyone's okay.

comments.name: Orange & Blue
comments.body: This is GREAT writing about connecting to a once unfamiliar sport with the enthusiasm of the newly converted, especially considering the big pull of a huge world-wide tournament that dwarfs all others! It is in large part because so many nation's teams across the planet are competing that I really feel the unification of our world in our common enjoyment of the matches. And it's almost like our entertainment in the moments of viewing are what it's all about. As another new "football" watcher these thoughts in this article resonate. And WHAT a line! "...rewatching the Knicks’ OG Anunoby reaching for that NBA Finals tip-in like Michelangelo’s God giving life to Adam", referencing something else but no matter. [ my 'Orange and Blue' user name relates to my Knicks allegiance ] The vibes of this FIFA World Cup are infectious & exhilarating to me even though my knowledge of the game is severely lacking. I wish we could begin it all over again so I can study and revel in it without having to wait another 4 years for the next World Cup!!

comments.name: mary
comments.body: If you really want to be moved by the entire experience, watch the Neil Diamond "Coming to America" video (find it on Youtube) of the world cup. Actually brought me to tears

comments.name: Sully
comments.body: And don’t forget the Scottish drinking Boston dry! No Scotland, No Party!

comments.name: Sergei Pontoise
comments.body: While I love soccer, Mr Poniewozik shows you don't have to love the sport to enjoy the experience, the mixing of cultures, etc. Just look at that photo of the Norway fans by the Times's Vincent Alban -- most folks with a goofy grin, recognizing in the moment the ridiculousness of it and in on the joke. And there's that guy who shows up to Belgium's games dressed like Obelix. American fans could learn to be more self-deprecating.

comments.name: Jewel
comments.body: I am somewhat like you - I don't watch or follow any sport, I don't have a favorite team...but my 13 year old is mad for soccer, and our entire family has fallen hook, line, and sinker for this World Cup.  We have tuned into almost every match, been to watch parties, the Fan Fest in our town, held signs up outside England's home base, and were even lucky enough to go to one group stage match together.  It has been a football summer and we have had such a wonderful time with each other, and our community.  I will miss it.

comments.name: Lisa Murphy
comments.body: 10th World Cup….became a fan 40 years ago watching my beloved Dutch team…while living the good life in the Netherlands. Nothing like it…drama..heartache..unreasonable hope..glorious fandom…it’s over now..almost…and life can resume….

comments.name: Inaka
comments.body:
Welcome to the bandwagon. Even in somewhere like the UK where it’s our main sport there are still plenty of people (like me) who only dip in for the World Cups. They’re fun! It’s special to enjoy this time every four years. 

I’m Scottish so this one was even more fun. The last time I actually went to a pub to watch a match it was Scotland going out in 1998. There was a minute of silent sadness after the whistle, then someone started singing and soon we were all in a congo line dancing round the pub. Best losers in the world :)

articles.title: Has the World Cup Turned Me Into … a Sports Guy?

comments.name: Here
comments.body:
"Toi, toi, toi!"

Ha ha ha, in the context of an opera being produced in France, when I first read that sentence, I thought the director had gone mad and went from door to door confronting each singer accusingly with:

"You, you, you!" 

Not unlike the "Toi!... Toi!" in Pelléas et Mélisande, when 
she is confronted by her suspicious and jealous husband, or the "Tu!... Tu!" in Tosca before she gets around gutting Scarpia, or the "Du! Du!" in Salome as she addresses Jochanaan, and we all know how THAT ends, so...

Phew! What a relief when I continued reading.

comments.name: Opera curious
comments.body:
This article has a faint whiff of “the gentleman doth protest too much.” It seems determined to build the Ted Huffman legend brick by brick, even if a couple of them feels a bit crumbly.

“Decent high school French”? Really? That may get you through ordering lunch in Provence, but general director of the Festival d’Aix-en-Provence feels like quite a stretch.

And the post-Yale table waiting? Yes, the college is Yale University. Trying to earn a starving-artist merit badge here? Huffman is very accomplished. And he also has led a fairly privileged life from a young age. So what? None of us gets to choose our birth family.

The reporter was clearly charmed. This reader remains unconvinced, though admittedly entertained.

comments.name: Here
comments.body:
"he showed both great humility, a capacity to adapt to circumstances that is quite rare without badmouthing..."

That's how I feel about how Esa-Pekka Salonen, a frequent and celebrated collaborator at Aix-en-Provence, should've dealt with San Francisco, instead of vociferously quitting the orchestra  by lambasting its board for failing to finance his artistic vision; well, things change, money falls short, that is just life, and more so in classical music than in other fields. I'm sure Salonen could've adapted in San Francisco just as he surely re-adapts at Aix-en-Provence, as circumstances require.

comments.name: Paulette
comments.body: Ted, wishing you all the best in this new exciting opportunity.

comments.name: Commentary2
comments.body: The opera expression rendered here as "toi, toi, toi" is said to be based on the belief that bad luck can be dissipated by saying the name of the devil three times.  The only language that I am aware of that sounds like that is German:  "Teufel".  So maybe the best way to render it in print would be "teu, teu, teu."

The review of The Dating Game exposes the profound arrogance of state-level social engineering. The creators of the One-Child Policy treated a population of over a billion people like a math equation on a chalkboard, completely ignoring basic human nature, deep-seated cultural preferences, and the simple reality of biology.

The knock-on effect will lift the economy and incomes, so taxes will rise. ... Or, just keep buying from the Chinese. comments.name: AG
comments.body: If there were no other buyers and the Chinese were shutting it down the plant was effectively being abandoned. Worthless to anyone but the UK. The government nationalizing it now rather than endless litigation and cleaning up a rotting toxic mess later is a win win for all involved.

comments.body: It would be interesting to know more about how this works. Do government officials swoop into private companies and tell them that there’s a new owner of the company? At least with GM, the company’s board agreed to the government bailout.

comments.name: longsummer
comments.body:
Jingye was funded by the Chinese state to take over the Scunthorpe plant and shut it down in order to end British independent steel production, reduce competition in the European steel market and increase British dependency on imported Chinese steel.

The story of this intervention to prevent Jingye turning off the blast furnaces would be worthy of a James Bond plot, with elements of "The Full Monty" woven in.

Steelworkers physically blocked senior Jingye managers from their offices in the steelworks and called in Humberside Police, who forced the Jingye executives to leave.

The House of Commons was recalled for an emergency Saturday sitting to pass legislation to prevent Jingye's attempt to shut down the blast furnaces summarily and the raw material supplies required to keep the furnaces working were secured by Department of Trade intervention.

At the time Jingye were demanding payment of their operating costs of £1.3m per day (per day!) to keep the furnaces working, so their claim for compensation for avoiding the obligation to keep the plant open is rather far-fetched.

comments.name: Norm Weaver
comments.body: I hope they succeed. The free world needs to make it's own steel, not buy it from China. The Chinese economic python squeezes the lifeblood out of everyone else's economy.

comments.name: Liemba
comments.body: It appears that the private owner of British Steel was going to close down the steel mill with no prospective buyer on the horizon. I would have thought the government might have been able to buy the entity at a very reasonable price if it had been purchased from the bankruptcy liquidation, assuming that’s where it was headed and if I am not mistaken. I wonder if the decision to nationalize British Steel resulted in part from political pressure and optics, given the timing of the event. Or perhaps the decision resulted from something much more noble than financial or political reasons. It may have been a good decision if the goal was to protect and preserve the brand and goodwill value of British Steel as a matter of national pride and tradition - though I would think it probably shouldn't have been sold to a foreign buyer in the first place then. Thank you for the interesting read.

This season's weather anomoly however means an early harvest and a reduced yield forced by nature. Not the worst news actually.

I just bought a Washington Cabernet that the winery retails for $45 marked down to $9.97 at Costco.

I bought a bunch of others a my local Pavilions (surprisingly good wine selection and prices) that were being closed out at 80% off retail.

A friend was recently offered basically unlimited cases of 2017 (18?) Beringer Private Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon for $70...winery is selling for $175.

But it's a great time to be a consumer...for wineries and winemakers, the future is very cloudy.

"Success often walks a tense tight rope."

Nice opening line. Probably the most literary and true thing in the Times today

comments.name: Bob

Wishing the family luck in pursuing the idea of a lifestyle and its values---they are clearly not actually committed to any place. Over the many generations of winemaking families across Europe, there have been good times and bad times, war and peace. And the seasonal rituals of a rural lifestyle. 

I'm not sure exactly what they are chasing, but you certainly can't buy it. And if your business plan needs a retail outlet, doesn't it make sense to check zoning regulations first before diving in? 

It takes many decades in a place to achieve the dream they are pursuing. Probably worth settling down to start living it.

comments.name: Jim Koch
comments.body: Such a fascinating article, showing the human story behind the bottle on the shelves.  Asimov does a wonderful job in describing the struggles and triumphs of these small wine producers in the context of the issues facing independent producers in the wine industry as a whole while also offering insight into the quality of the wines themselves.  A wonderful example of the knowledgeable, well-reported and (most importantly)  interesting articles his readers have come to expect from him.  One of the rare wine columnists who brings as much passion to the humanity of the producers and the state of the industry as a whole as he does to a tasting.

comments.name: Joseph
comments.body: I wish them the best of luck, and I look forward to trying their wines someday—and maybe meeting them. I'm heading to Bordeaux this coming week. Despite it being so unfashionable, for all the wrong reasons, there's still much good wine being made by small, independent producers, and a good amount of it is now organic, biodynamic, or both, for those of us seeking low-intervention wines (see how I avoided saying "natural" just now?). Bordeaux, the city, is loaded with great wine bars, excellent restaurants, and plenty of culture to keep you engaged. And let's not forget, in this weather, the incredible beaches just west of the city.

comments.name: Etaoin Shrdlu
comments.body:
Unions have the sole and exclusive right to represent their members under the NYC Collective Bargaining Law.  The Local Law that granted "uniformed" status to ÈMS did nothing to change the duty to bargain, nor did it magically confer benefits on these employees.  It did remove them from coverage under the Citywide Agreement negotiated by DC 37, but the same benefits continue to apply unless and until they bargain something different although not necessarily better.
The City should review why the trades are still covered under Section 220 of the Labor Law.  That provision gives those Unions the option to bargain the same as other Municipal employees, or to seek a litigated determination from the Comptroller's Office, whichever is better.  NYS did away with this archaic provision, established during the Great Depression, years ago for its own employees.  NYC is still on the hook.

Venice may denser than any place other than Rome - even more than Florence - with art still situated where it was originally planned to situated. (And it's certainly far easier to get around than Rome unless you cannot navigate bridge steps.) Venice is the quintessentially perfect place to wander and explore without any plan other than curiousity (and - except when there are big cruise ships around - to be rewarded by an auralscape NOT dominated by mechanical sounds but instead by natural and human sounds).

Art and art history people, for whom a museum-based view of things is so foundational, may not fully appreciate the magic of this wonder: 

to go into a space not filled with artificial light, 

to find masterpieces and near-masterpieces in all sorts of nooks and crannies in addition to obvious spots, usually in a jumble with many other objects and furnishings and architectural elements into which they were designed to be placed, 

to be forced to seek and not have everything laid out pre-sorted and pre-masticated, and 

for religious/sacred artworks, to see them their true context as intended, not isolated on a sterile museum wall or floor. 

One of the magical things about the Basilica San Marco in the off-season during aqua alta is, if you can manage to be inside during Mass without much in the way of the sounds of heavy tourist tramping on elevated ramps, the hear the magnificence of the acoustics working like an instrument, with the bonus feature of water sounds.

When it comes to the hard work of lowering greenhouse gas emissions, the answer is... not nearly as many as you might like to believe. 

To report this story, I researched companies across industries that had pledged to combat climate change. What I found was a mixed bag. While many companies are still trying to make progress, realizing some of their most audacious goals has been challenging.

What are your thoughts on big business's efforts to fight climate change? If you work at a company that has been trying to reduce emissions, what's the story there?

I live in Chicago. Today we are experiencing our worst Air Quality index ever due to the Ontario fires. I am 73. We never had this type of situation until a few years ago. Why can’t people believe the science and their own eyes and ears about climate change? Why can’t they believe their own eyes and ears, given all that is going on around them?
We keep experiencing more and more extreme weather events each year. More ice cap and snow cap melting, affecting the world’s future water supply. We can see this right here in our western states. 
More ocean warming, negatively affecting thousands of species sea life and causing the ocean level to rise. We can see these in Miami, where water can bubble up through the streets even when it’s not raining.
More desertification of once fertile lands around the world, causing huge immigration waves of people who cannot survive anymore in their current location.  
Land habitats are changing, leading to the reduction in and often extinction of many species of birds, animals, and insects.  
More extreme wild fires, storms, and flooding occurring, costing billions of dollars. 
There are many more climate change adverse effects I could list and the situation is only worsening from year to year. I am very, very afraid for my nieces and nephews and their grandchildren. Actually, for all the younger people in this world. I’m one of the lucky ones. Hopefully I will be dead before the immensely catastrophic effects are felt.

Smoke is not small particles, it's gases consisting of very small molecules. The filters must be able to remove the molecules from the air.
